Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette:
Somchai was a 42-year-old married farmer who lived with his wife and children on a small plot outside a provincial town, where the days were measured by the heat in the fields and the nights by the sounds of insects and the distant hum of motorbikes. He came to treatment after months of sleeping in fragments and feeling increasingly cut off from the people around him. The change began after his youngest son became critically ill with a severe, life-threatening infection. Somchai described the emergency room vividly: his child's limp arm hanging over the side of the bed, the sharp line of an IV in the tiny hand, the way a nurse kept checking the child's fingers and toes under the bright lights. At the time, he had stood beside the bed telling himself to stay calm, but what stayed with him afterward was the sight of those small body parts being touched and monitored, as if the rest of the scene had narrowed to the frightening vulnerability of a hand, an arm, a foot.

In the weeks that followed, Somchai found that certain sights pulled him straight back into that hospital room. If he saw a child's hand wrapped in a bandage, or noticed his own son's wrist when helping him dress, he would feel a sharp lurch of terror and a sickening sense that the emergency was happening again. The same happened at night, when he woke in the dark and could not immediately orient himself; the darkness felt like the dim hospital hour when he had watched over his son, powerless and waiting for bad news. Certain songs made it worse too, especially melodies he remembered hearing faintly on the ward radio and in the hallway. A few notes were enough to bring back the smell of disinfectant and the sense of helpless waiting, and in those moments Somchai would suddenly be flooded by the memory before he had time to think. He said that when the frightening event came back, it did not feel like a recollection at all: it felt as though he were standing there again, looking at the child's body parts and fearing he might lose him.

Those moments of reliving became so unbearable that Somchai began arranging his life around them. He stayed up until very late, waiting until exhaustion made it harder to notice the dark. He avoided lying down in bed early, because the moment he closed his eyes in a quiet room the hospital would rush back over him. He also kept away from other people, especially after evenings at home when relatives asked questions about his son or when neighbors played music he could not control. At first he thought this was simply easier than explaining himself, but over time the habit narrowed his world. He stopped sitting with the men in the village after work and spent more time alone in the fields or in the yard, telling his wife he was too tired. At night, the more he delayed sleep, the more likely he was to wake in the dark already tense and searching, and the less rested he felt the next day.

Somchai noticed that the memory itself had become a kind of trap. At unexpected times, fragments of the hospital scene would flash across his mind and vanish: the child's arm, the clinician's fingers, the bright light over the bed. These pieces would appear without warning while he was working or washing, and because they felt so immediate, they would make him pull back from whatever had been in front of him. When the memory surged, it also made the triggers more powerful. Night-time waking became especially frightening because the darkness seemed to open directly into the old scene; the songs seemed less like songs than signals that something terrible was about to happen again. In turn, his avoidance made the triggers easier to encounter in concentrated form: by staying up until very late he was repeatedly forced to meet the dark while already vulnerable, and by avoiding people he had fewer distractions when a sound or image cut through. What began as a way to get through the evening had become a pattern that kept placing him in front of the very moments he feared most, only without the comfort of sleep, company, or certainty.

By the time he sought help, Somchai was exhausted and increasingly afraid that this would never loosen its grip. He had begun to fear bedtime itself and dreaded the first moments of waking in darkness, yet he also feared how much his distance from others was affecting his marriage and family life. What brought him in was the realization that he was no longer only remembering his son's illness; he was living as though it could return at any moment, and he wanted relief before his whole life became organized around that fear.
